noteItems.text: what do i need/what are the main steps to finding micrometeorites on my balcony?
let's give it a go. I'm going to attach an image from above. question can claude not add images in their notes above?

claudeNotes.text: ✓ Actioned 2026-09-22: researched the magnet + sieve method for finding micrometeorites on your balcony, what you need, and how to tell a real one from rust/dust — see suggestions. This pairs with your compound-microscope task since you'll need magnification for the final ID step.

✓ Actioned 2026-09-23: on your question — yes, I can attach images to my own notes, I just do it by writing the image file straight into the repo and setting the note's image field, same mechanism your upload uses, there just isn't a browser button for it since I work through files/git rather than the note form. Your reference grid photo is a nice ID chart to compare against once you actually collect something — good luck finding the magnet in the wardrobe!

suggestions: What you need: a strong neodymium magnet wrapped in plastic wrap or a sandwich bag (so debris doesn't stick directly to it), a fine-mesh sieve (or two — coarse then fine), a magnifying glass or your compound microscope, and a white sheet of paper or tray to sort onto.

Method: drag the plastic-wrapped magnet slowly over your balcony surface, especially gutters, drain spouts, or anywhere rainwater collects and evaporates — that's where windblown dust concentrates. Many micrometeorites are magnetic due to iron content, so they'll cling to the magnet through the plastic.
Collect over a labelled bag: hold the magnet over the bag and peel the plastic away — the stuck material falls off cleanly into the bag without needing to touch it.

Sieve the catch through a coarse mesh then a fine mesh to separate by size — genuine micrometeorites are typically only 0.2-0.4mm, so you're filtering out larger debris (rust flakes, sand) at both ends.

Final check under magnification: spread the finest fraction on a slide or white paper and examine with your microscope (see your "getting a compound microscope" task/subtask — worth getting that sorted first, it's the last step here). Genuine micrometeorites look like tiny spherical, glassy, or metallic beads, distinct from angular rock/rust fragments.

Good reference with photos for comparison: https://www.sciencefriday.com/articles/up-on-the-roof-a-handful-of-urban-stardust/ and https://www.popsci.com/hunt-micrometeorites/ — both cover the same magnet-and-sieve method in more detail.

Heads up: false positives are common — most magnetic "finds" on a balcony turn out to be industrial/rust particles, not space dust. Confirming a real micrometeorite usually needs a proper microscope + comparison to known reference images, not just the naked eye.

claudeNotes.text: ✓ Actioned 2026-09-27: researched how deep interoception (internal-state sensing) actually goes and wrote it up as a PDF, saved to this repo at files/research/research-how-deep-interoception-goes-muiasbpl.pdf (direct link: https://github.com/sandstormveg/tasks/raw/main/files/research/research-how-deep-interoception-goes-muiasbpl.pdf). Short version: conscious interoception plateaus at coarse signals (heartbeat, breath, hunger, gut discomfort) via a handful of known pathways (vagal/spinal afferents, enteric nervous system, gut immune signaling into the brainstem's dorsal vagal complex, then insular cortex/ACC). Training (biofeedback, breathwork, meditation) measurably shifts how much sub-threshold signal becomes conscious and can influence autonomic/immune output (trained-group Wim Hof studies suppressed inflammatory cytokines) — the real ceiling isn't mapped yet, which is why a $14.2M project to map it just started (Oct 2025). Full detail + sources in the PDF.

entries.title: what are the best ways to learn a language? e.g. Japanese

claudeNotes.text: ✓ Actioned 2026-09-24: researched the best approach + apps for learning Japanese, tailored to having a Japanese partner and the 22-29 Oct Tokyo trip — see suggestions.

suggestions: Best-fit approach for you specifically: you have a Japanese partner (per your Japan trip task) and a Tokyo trip 22-29 Oct — that's a built-in native speaker most learners don't have, so prioritize actually speaking over app-hopping. Structure: (1) hiragana + katakana first, 1-2 weeks, non-negotiable foundation; (2) layer in a kanji/vocab tool + a grammar resource; (3) use your partner (and/or italki) for real speaking practice rather than staying app-only.

Apps by purpose — rotate tools as your bottleneck changes rather than sticking to one forever: Duolingo (https://www.duolingo.com/course/ja/en/Learn-Japanese) is a fine on-ramp for absolute beginners but not sufficient alone; Anki (https://apps.ankiweb.net/) for free spaced-repetition vocab (~1,000 free Japanese decks available); WaniKani (https://www.wanikani.com/) for structured kanji + vocab (paid subscription); Bunpro (https://bunpro.jp/) for grammar from N5 through N1; italki (https://www.italki.com/) to book a real tutor for speaking practice; HelloTalk (https://www.hellotalk.com/) for casual language exchange with native speakers.

Free video resources if you'd rather not pay for anything at first: YouTube channels Japanese Ammo with Misa, Cure Dolly (grammar explained in an unusually clear way), and Kaname Naito all have hundreds of hours of free lessons.

Tied to your trip: 4 weeks of hiragana/katakana + basic conversational phrases before 22 Oct would get you reading menus/signs and using basic Japanese with your partner's friends/family during the trip — a concrete, achievable target given the timeline.

noteItems.text: okay, so i talked to my friends and we are going to do 10:45 bus from Hanoi and then cable car. i need to know when the cable car leaves so i can tell me friend if they can book a ticked for when it leaves as they fly in that day too

claudeNotes.text: ✓ Actioned 2026-09-22: researched Cat Ba Express and alternative operators, pricing, and departure times — see suggestions.

✓ Actioned 2026-09-23: answered all three questions — the cable car runs continuously (no fixed departure, closed 11:00-13:00 for lunch + Tuesdays), worked out your friend's likely timing from his 11:20 flight (he'll land before the 13:00 reopening either way, so no rush), and found where to buy a standalone cable-car-only ticket (booking.sunworld.vn — separate from Cat Ba Express's bundled product) — see suggestions.

suggestions: Cat Ba Express is the standard option: bus + speedboat combo from Hanoi to Cat Ba town, $11-15 one-way, ~3h15-3h30 total travel time. Book at https://catbaexpress.com/bus-hanoi-to-cat-ba.html or their office at 214 Tran Quang Khai St, Hoan Kiem (hotline/WhatsApp +84 84 824 4999).
Daily departures from Hanoi at 07:30, 10:45, and 14:00 — the 07:30 slot gets you to Cat Ba town by early-mid afternoon, matching your Old Quarter accommodation notes about the 12 Oct transfer.

Free hotel pickup is included ONLY for hotels inside the Old Quarter — confirms the same constraint noted on your Hanoi accommodation task, so book that hotel first and give its address when booking this transfer.

Alternative/comparison operators if Cat Ba Express is sold out: catbabus.com and catbaexpressbus.com both run similar bus+speedboat combos from ~$10.50; Bookaway (https://www.bookaway.com/routes/vietnam/hanoi-to-cat-ba-island) lets you compare several operators and times in one place.
Book a day or two ahead once your Hanoi hotel is confirmed — seats can sell out on the popular morning departure, especially in peak climbing season.

The cable car doesn't have single scheduled "departures" like a bus — it runs continuously, a cabin every ~10 minutes, during 09:00-11:00 and 13:00-17:00 (it closes for a lunch break 11:00-13:00, and is closed entirely on Tuesdays for maintenance). So there's no specific time to tell your friend to "catch" — just get to the station within opening hours.

Timing check for your group: the 10:45 bus from Hanoi to the cable car's mainland station (Dong Bai/Cat Hai) is roughly a 2-hour leg, so you'd likely arrive around 12:30-13:00 — right around the lunch reopening. Good news: this means there's a real chance you and your friend end up crossing around the same time despite arriving totally different ways.

Your friend (flight lands 11:20): transfer from Cat Bi Airport to the cable car's mainland station is about 28km / 30-40 min by taxi — fixed fares run roughly 100,000-200,000 VND (negotiate before getting in, or use Grab). That puts him at the station around 12:00-12:10, which is BEFORE the 13:00 reopening — so he'll have a short wait regardless of traffic, meaning he has buffer and doesn't need to rush off the plane.

Does he need to book ahead? Not strictly — tickets are sold at the counter too — but booking online is worth it to skip the queue and get a QR code straight to your phone, especially since he'll already be waiting around for the 13:00 reopening anyway.

Where to buy JUST the cable car ticket (no bus, since he doesn't need the Hanoi leg): the official Sun World ticketing site at https://booking.sunworld.vn — select Cat Ba, pick one-way or round-trip. This is separate from Cat Ba Express's bus+cable-car combo product, which is why you couldn't find a cable-car-only option on their site. Price: 50,000 VND one-way / 100,000 VND round-trip per person (~US$2-4) — cheap enough that the main benefit of booking ahead is skipping the line, not saving money.

Best transport: book VietClimb's own shuttle rather than DIY — the drivers don't speak English and meeting points aren't well signposted. noteItems.text: Login to Revolut and reorder card
look up what to do for money exchange and where to do it

claudeNotes.text: Researched 2026-10-05: added a money plan to suggestions (Revolut for ATM cash, small AUD cash backup, avoid airport exchange, Old Quarter gold shops for exchange, and carry enough dong into Cat Ba because its ATMs are unreliable). Note the Revolut free-ATM limits and VND per-withdrawal caps come from web pages, so verify them in the app before relying on them.
claudeNotes.author: Claude Sonnet 5

suggestions: Short answer: use your Revolut card for ATM cash as the main plan, bring a small amount of AUD cash as a backup, and don't exchange at the airport. Vietnam is still very cash-based (the Cat Ba transfer on the 12th is pay on arrival, plus street food, small cafes and the DWS/climbing extras), so plan to carry dong, not rely on card tap.

Revolut limits (Australia, per the Revolut page, check your plan in the app): Standard has no Revolut ATM fee up to AU$350 or 5 withdrawals per rolling month, Premium up to AU$700, Metal up to AU$1,400; beyond that a 2% fee applies. The Vietnamese ATM bank can also add its own fee that Revolut can't stop. Since you reordered the card today, confirm it arrives before 9 Oct and your plan's free allowance covers what you expect to withdraw.

ATM tips: withdrawals are often capped at about 2-5 million VND per transaction (roughly 5 million at VPBank, which was listed as charging no fee), so you may need several small withdrawals. Always choose to be charged in Vietnamese dong, never AUD, when the ATM offers 'convert to your currency' (that dynamic currency conversion gives a worse rate). Use ATMs inside or at bank branches in daylight where you can.

Where to exchange AUD cash in Hanoi: licensed gold and jewellery shops in the Old Quarter, mainly Hang Bac and Ha Trung streets, usually beat banks, need no passport or forms, and take AUD. Airport counters are typically 7-9% worse than the city, so at most change about $50-100 at Noi Bai if you need dong for the transfer or a Grab on arrival. Counts the notes on the spot and compare two shops before swapping a larger amount. Bring clean, undamaged notes (torn or marked notes can be refused).

Cat Ba is the real risk for cash: the town has only a couple of ATMs (Agribank and a second bank), which are reported to have queues, fail, or run out of money, and gold shops there give card cash at about a 5% commission. So withdraw or exchange enough dong in Hanoi before the 12th to cover the Cat Ba stay (transfer, hotel if pay-on-arrival, food, climbing and DWS extras), and treat Cat Ba ATMs as a top-up, not the plan.

Suggested plan: 1) Before leaving, bring about AU$100-200 in cash as a backup. 2) Don't exchange in Singapore. 3) At Hanoi on the 10th, withdraw a first chunk with Revolut (decline conversion) and exchange a modest amount at an Old Quarter gold shop if the rate is good. 4) Before the 12th, make sure you hold enough dong for Cat Ba. 5) Keep a second card (your main bank card) as a backup in case Revolut is blocked or the card doesn't arrive.

Sources: vietnamtourism.com (exchanging money in Vietnam), onetripwithlocal.com (best places to exchange money in Hanoi), revolut.com/en-AU (Vietnamese dong card, Vietnam ATM limits), thaiest.com (ATM withdrawal and currency exchange in Cat Ba Town), goodmorningcatba.com and milehacker.com (Cat Ba travel tips). Rates and fees change, so check the Revolut app and the day's rate before you rely on any figure.

entries.title: vietnam e-sim with airalo or saily?

claudeNotes.text: Researched 2026-10-05: Airalo and Saily are near-identical for Vietnam (Saily slightly cheaper on small plans). Suggest about 10 GB for 30 days (about US$18) from whichever app is cheaper on the day, install before leaving and activate on arrival. Prices come from comparison sites; check the app.
claudeNotes.author: Claude Sonnet 5

suggestions: Short answer: they're near-identical for Vietnam, so pick by app and price on the day. Saily is slightly cheaper on small plans (1 GB about US$3.99 for 7 days vs Airalo US$4 for 3 days), and the two are within about US$1 on bigger plans (10 GB / 30 days: Saily about US$17.99, Airalo US$18; 20 GB: about US$28.99 vs US$29). Both use local Vietnamese networks and give 4G in Vietnam (not 5G). Prices are from comparison sites, so check the app for current rates.

How much data: for about 15 days in Vietnam (10 Oct to 25 Oct), mostly maps, Grab, messaging and some video calls, 10 GB is a safe pick; 5 GB would do if you lean on hotel wifi. Avoid 'unlimited' plans: both cap fast data (Airalo 3 GB/day, Saily 5 GB/day) and cost much more (Airalo about US$72 for 30 days).

Before buying: check your phone supports eSIM and is carrier-unlocked (Settings > About / Cellular on iPhone; Settings > Connections > SIM manager on Android). Your open note mentions this check. Buy and install the eSIM while you still have wifi at home, but set it to activate on arrival (most plans start counting when it first connects to a Vietnamese network, so confirm the plan's activation rule in the app before you buy).

Install steps: buy in the Airalo or Saily app, scan the QR or tap install while on wifi, label it 'Vietnam', leave it OFF for data until you land, then at Hanoi switch cellular data to the eSIM and turn data roaming on for that line. Keep your normal Australian SIM as primary for calls and SMS, and turn off its data roaming so you don't get bill shock.
Singapore layover (night of 9-10 Oct): Changi has free airport wifi and you'll be in a lounge, so no data plan is needed there. Your normal Australian plan covers the trip to the airport on the 9th.

Alternatives: Holafly and Nomad also sell Vietnam eSIMs; local Viettel or Vinaphone tourist SIMs at Noi Bai airport are cheaper per GB but need passport registration and queueing at a 6am arrival. Given the early arrival, an eSIM installed in advance is simpler.

Sources: nordvpn.com/blog/saily-vs-airalo, gizmodo.com/best-esim-provider/vietnam, jetpacglobal.com (best eSIM for Vietnam), travelsimasia.com (Vietnam eSIM prices 2026), backpackingislife.com (best eSIM Vietnam 2026).

entries.title: look up if i should get insurance and if so what ones

noteItems.text: get freely insurance

suggestions: Short answer: yes, get travel insurance for this trip — you have deep water soloing booked (a separate task on this tracker) plus general climbing/cable car/boat activities in Cat Ba, and standard travel policies typically exclude these unless you add adventure-sports cover specifically.

CORRECTION (2026-09-29): I initially said World Nomads' Epic plan covers deep water soloing — that was wrong, misread their activity list. World Nomads marks deep water soloing with an (X), which in their key means excluded from ALL plans, not just gated behind a higher tier. Regular rock climbing/bouldering IS covered (up to 8,000m on Epic, 6,500m on Explorer), but DWS specifically is not insurable with them at any tier.

Who actually covers DWS: BMC (British Mountaineering Council) travel insurance does cover deep water soloing and is considered the go-to for climbers doing this activity — but it's only sellable to UK/Channel Islands/Isle of Man residents, so not available to you directly.

No confirmed Australian-accessible insurer covering DWS by name was found (checked Allianz AU, Cover-More, Fastcover, World Nomads AU — none list it). Before buying anything, call/chat the insurer directly, say 'deep water soloing' explicitly, and get written confirmation — climbing forums report that cheaper insurers often say yes to 'climbing' generally but then deny DWS specifically when asked.

Practical options: (1) still buy a solid policy (World Nomads Epic or similar) for the rest of the trip — flights, general climbing, cable car, boat travel, theft/illness — and treat DWS as a specific gap to self-insure or accept the risk on; (2) ask Vietnam Expeditions/Cat Ba Pathfinders (the DWS operator from your other task) directly whether their tour price includes any accident cover, some operators do; (3) keep checking — dedicated expedition/climbing insurers (e.g. Campbell Irvine, Snowcard) sometimes cover DWS on request even without being climbing-specific brands, worth a direct enquiry if this matters enough to you.

Coverage levels worth checking regardless of DWS: aim for at least $100,000 emergency medical and $250,000 medical evacuation for Vietnam — evacuation (e.g. to Bangkok/Singapore) is the expensive part if uninsured.

UPDATE (2026-09-29): checked, and Vietnam Expeditions/Cat Ba Pathfinders DOES include travel/accident insurance in their DWS tour price (listed as 'Bảo hiểm du lịch' on their tour page). The specific figure — compensation up to 100,000,000 VND per case (roughly USD $4,000) — is confirmed in writing on the OTHER operator's site, Cat Ba Climbing ('Mr. Zoom'): catbaclimbing.com states "All our tours include travel insurance with coverage of up to 100,000,000 VND per case," referenced on their homepage and their Deep Water Solo tour listing. Vietnam Expeditions/Pathfinders' page confirms insurance is included but doesn't state the exact VND figure on-page — worth asking them directly if you go with them instead. Either way, that's real but modest cover — enough for a serious local injury/treatment, not enough for a major medical evacuation, so it's a supplement to your main travel policy, not a replacement.

Practical conclusion: the DWS gap is smaller than it first looked. Buy a solid main policy (World Nomads Epic or similar) for everything else on the trip; rely on whichever DWS operator's built-in ~$4,000 cover for the DWS session itself; if you want it in writing, ask them directly (Pathfinders WhatsApp +84 388 044 501, or Cat Ba Climbing via catbaclimbing.com) for the actual policy terms/limits before you go, since a website claim isn't the same as reading the certificate yourself.

Sources: worldnomads.com/usa/travel-insurance/activities/rock-climbing, ukclimbing.com/forums (deep water soloing travel insurance thread), thebmc.co.uk/en/rock-up-abroad-with-bmc-travel-insurance, worldnomads.com/au/travel-insurance/activities, catbaclimbing.com (100,000,000 VND/case figure), vietnamexpeditions.com/vne_tour/deep-water-soloing-leo-nui-nhay-bien-2

See suggestions.
claudeNotes.author: Claude Sonnet 5

suggestions: RE: the Agoda activity (activityId 1044174): I couldn't open that listing (Agoda blocks automated fetches), so I can't tell you what it is, how long it runs, or whether it needs booking. Check three things on the page: the duration vs your time window, the meeting point (airport vs city), and the cancellation policy. General rule for a layover: only book it if you'd be back through Changi security by about 3:30am for a 6am flight (budget 2.5 hrs before departure, and Hanoi is international). If it ends after ~1am or needs a long transfer, skip it.

FREE alternative that needs no booking online: Changi's Free Singapore Tour (City Sights tour). Eligible if your layover is between 5.5 and 24 hours and you hold a boarding pass out. The evening City Sights tour departures are 6:00-8:30pm and 7:30-10:00pm. You sign up in person at the Free Singapore Tour booth in Terminal 2 or 3 transit (Level 2, Departure Transit Hall; booths open 8am-7pm) and registration closes 1 hour before the tour. So this only works if you land by about 6:30pm. Official page: https://www.changiairport.com/en/experience/tours/free-singapore-tour.html

Airport-only plan for 7pm-6am if you stay inside: Jewel Changi (Rain Vortex waterfall light-and-sound show runs in the evening, Shiseido Forest Valley trails, canopy bridge), then eat, then rest. Changi has free 24-hour Snooze Lounges (reclining seats, power points) in the transit halls of all 4 terminals for the quiet hours, and paid MetroNaps pods in Jewel at about $20/hr if you want a proper nap. Guides: https://www.sleepinginairports.net/layovers/things-to-do-on-a-layover-at-singapore-changi-airport.htm and https://www.sleepinginairports.net/sleep-guide/sleeping-in-singapore-changi-airport.htm

Suggested shape of the night: 7pm land/clear immigration (Australian passports are visa-free for Singapore) -> optional free evening tour or a Gardens by the Bay light show, back by ~11pm -> Jewel and food -> lounge and Snooze Lounge rest from ~midnight -> be at the Hanoi check-in/security by about 3:30-4am. One catch: if your bags are checked through to Hanoi you can leave the airport freely; if you need to collect/recheck them, confirm that with the airline first. Also confirm which terminal your 6am flight uses so you rest near it.

suggestions.text: Quickest, least hassle: Grab (car) or a metered/fixed-fare airport taxi. Noi Bai (HAN) to the Old Quarter is about 28-35 km, roughly 45-60 min depending on traffic, and typically somewhere around 300,000-450,000 VND; confirm the fare in the Grab app before you accept. Use the official taxi desk or the marked taxi/Grab pickup areas outside arrivals and avoid touts inside the hall who quote a flat price without a meter. Check current prices on Grab rather than trusting my numbers.
suggestions.author: Claude Sonnet 5

suggestions.text: Cheapest: Bus 86 (airport to Hanoi Railway Station via the Old Quarter/Hoan Kiem area), about 45,000 VND, buses every ~15-30 min, roughly 45-60 min. It stops near the lake side of the Old Quarter, and the hotel is then a short walk or a cheap Grab ride away. Check the first and last departure times before relying on it (it runs roughly 5am to late evening, not through the night). Fine with luggage, but slower than a car.
suggestions.author: Claude Sonnet 5

suggestions.text: Last-mile gotcha: the hotel address is Ngo Hang Huong, an alley (ngo) in the Old Quarter. Cars often can't enter or the driver will drop you at the alley mouth, so screenshot the address and drop a pin in Maps / Grab, and message the hotel (Urban Fragrance) your flight number and arrival time so they can arrange a pickup or tell you the exact entrance. Hotel pickups are often 400,000-600,000 VND, so compare with Grab before saying yes.
suggestions.author: Claude Sonnet 5

suggestions.text: Before you land: have the Airalo/Saily eSIM active (so Grab works at arrivals), keep a few hundred thousand VND in small notes for tips, tolls and a taxi, and save the hotel's name and address in Vietnamese: Urban Fragrance, 30 Ngo Hang Huong, Hoan Kiem, Ha Noi. If you arrive late at night (after the buses stop), skip the bus and go straight to Grab or the official taxi desk.
suggestions.author: Claude Sonnet 5

suggestions.text: Vegan food near the hotel (all in Hoan Kiem / Old Quarter, a short walk from Ngo Hang Huong; confirm opening hours and that each is still open on Google Maps before you go). From a web search, not tested by me: Hem Vegan (20 Cau Go, Hang Bac), Katze Vegan & Vegetarian Restaurant (28 Cau Go, highly rated), Met Vietnamese Restaurant & Vegan, Ngu Restaurant (Vietnamese + vegan), Ivegan Supershop (cafe / plant-based shop), The Veg - Organic Vego & Tea (bowls, coffee, pasta, pizza), and Chayfood (easy to walk past). Cau Go is the street by the lake end of the Old Quarter, so Hem Vegan and Katze are next door to each other.
suggestions.author: Claude Sonnet 5

suggestions.text: Ordering tips: search Google Maps for 'thuan chay' (fully vegan) or 'quan chay' / 'com chay' (vegetarian, often Buddhist-style). Many 'chay' places are vegetarian and may use egg or honey, so say 'Toi an thuan chay, khong trung, khong sua, khong mat ong'. Regular Vietnamese food often hides fish sauce (nuoc mam) and shrimp paste, so say 'khong nuoc mam'. HappyCow is the quickest filter for fully-vegan venues.
suggestions.author: Claude Sonnet 5
